stem: A patient with myoclonic seizures was started on Valproic acid, but the seizures persist despite adequate treatment. What is the next appropriate medication to give?
key_concept:
Myoclonic seizure ladder.
  • First line: valproate (not in women of childbearing potential)
  • Next/alternative: levetiracetam
  • Avoid: phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin (worsen myoclonus)
  • Lamotrigine: good for focal/GTC, may worsen myoclonus
  • Ethosuximide: absence only
exam_pearl: Ethosuximide tempts only if you misread myoclonic as absence; sodium channel blockers (and sometimes lamotrigine) can worsen myoclonus.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: ACS 5 days after, gets hypotension, tachycardia, not ok, with pansystolic murmur radiating to right sternal border (yes it was Right not Lt).
why_right: A new harsh pansystolic murmur with hypotension and tachycardia about 5 days after MI is a mechanical complication. A holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border that radiates to the right sternal border is the acquired VSD murmur, so this is interventricular septal rupture (left to right shunt causing cardiogenic shock).
why_wrong_block:
A. Free wall rupture causes acute tamponade (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, PEA, sudden death) with NO new murmur.
C. A pseudoaneurysm is a contained free wall rupture, often silent or with heart failure and a to-and-fro murmur found on echo; it does not give a new pansystolic murmur radiating to the right sternal border.
key_concept:
Post-MI mechanical complications (typically days 3 to 5).
  • Septal rupture: pansystolic murmur at left sternal border, thrill, shock, O2 step-up in RV
  • Papillary muscle rupture: acute MR, apical murmur to axilla, flash pulmonary edema
  • Free wall rupture: tamponade, no murmur, PEA/sudden death
  • Pseudoaneurysm: contained rupture, needs surgery
  • Late LV aneurysm: persistent ST elevation weeks later
  • Confirm all with echocardiography
exam_pearl: Murmur heading to the STERNUM = septal rupture; murmur heading to the AXILLA with pulmonary edema = papillary muscle rupture.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option B printed as 'Atreoventricular septal rupture'.

stem: Patient had MI two years ago (PCI and stent), came to ER with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea at rest. Echo: EF 20%. Most appropriate management for the situation of the patient?
OptC: IV furosemide and NON invasive ventilation
highlight_terms_source: progressive dyspnea and orthopnea at rest
why_right: A post-MI patient with EF 20% and dyspnea and orthopnea at rest has acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema. The ER treatment is IV furosemide to offload fluid plus oxygenation; in respiratory distress, non-invasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP) improves oxygenation, reduces work of breathing and preload, and avoids intubation.
why_wrong_block:
A. These are chronic oral disease-modifying drugs; a beta blocker should not be started during acute decompensation, and propranolol is not an evidence-based HF beta blocker anyway.
B. Oral furosemide is too slow and poorly absorbed in a congested gut; the acute vasodilator would be nitrates if hypertensive, not IV hydralazine.
D. Intubation is for failure of NIV, reduced consciousness, exhaustion or refractory hypoxemia; it is not the first ventilatory step here.
key_concept:
ADHF in the ER: decongest and support breathing.
  • IV loop diuretic (furosemide)
  • Oxygen; NIV if respiratory distress or persistent hypoxemia
  • Nitrates if hypertensive
  • Inotropes if hypotensive/cardiogenic shock
  • Intubate only if NIV fails or patient cannot protect airway
  • Chronic GDMT (ACEi/ARNI, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) once stable
exam_pearl: "At rest" dyspnea in pulmonary edema = NIV; choose intubation only when the stem adds drowsiness, exhaustion or NIV failure.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option A printed as 'oral propranolol and ivasartan'. Answer line: IV furosemide and NON invasive ventilation.

stem: Patient with hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and end-stage kidney disease presents with muffled heart sounds. Echocardiogram shows pericardial effusion. BP: 86/... (Was Frankly Hypotensive) What is the Most Appropriate Next Step?
why_right: Muffled heart sounds, an echo-proven pericardial effusion and frank hypotension (BP 86) mean cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise. An unstable tamponade needs immediate drainage, so pericardiocentesis is the next step regardless of the underlying uremic cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Furosemide lowers preload, which a tamponaded heart depends on, and will worsen hypotension; an ESKD patient also responds poorly to diuretics. Tamponade is managed with fluids and drainage, not diuresis.
C. Intensive dialysis treats uremic pericarditis or effusion in a STABLE patient; here the patient is hypotensive, and fluid removal on dialysis could precipitate collapse, so drain first.
key_concept:
Pericardial effusion in ESKD: stability decides.
  • Beck triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP; plus pulsus paradoxus
  • Diagnosis: echocardiography
  • Unstable/tamponade: pericardiocentesis (or surgical drainage)
  • Stable uremic pericarditis/effusion: intensify dialysis
  • Avoid diuretics and vasodilators in tamponade
exam_pearl: Same uremic effusion with NORMAL BP = hemodialysis; add hypotension and it becomes pericardiocentesis.

stem: 60 years old man with history of HTN and DM, came with 4 months history of increased abdominal distention, no history of alcohol use, he reported 10 years history of high aminotransferase, upon examination he has ascites. No splenomegaly. What is the BEST?
why_right: The picture is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (HTN, DM, no alcohol, 10 years of raised aminotransferases) now presenting with ascites, suggesting progression to cirrhosis. This recall's key is liver biopsy because, read as "BEST", biopsy is the gold standard to confirm steatohepatitis, stage fibrosis/cirrhosis and exclude other causes of chronic transaminitis. The compiler and most guidelines note that biopsy is not routinely required.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ultrasound (with Doppler) is the initial non-invasive test for fatty liver, cirrhosis, ascites and portal hypertension; the compiler favours it as the next step, but it is not the gold standard the key is aiming at.
C. Abdominal CT adds radiation and contrast without helping diagnose steatosis or cirrhosis; multiphasic CT is used to characterise a liver nodule >1 cm found on ultrasound surveillance.
key_concept:
NAFLD/cirrhosis workup: initial vs gold standard.
  • New ascites: diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, cell count)
  • Initial imaging: ultrasound with Doppler
  • Fibrosis staging: non-invasive scores and elastography
  • Gold standard: liver biopsy, reserved for unclear diagnosis
  • Cirrhosis: ultrasound HCC surveillance; nodule >1 cm -> multiphasic CT/MRI
exam_pearl: The lead-in decides: "initial/next step" = ultrasound; "gold standard/confirm" = biopsy. This source key reads "BEST" as gold standard.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: This is a case of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease complicated by cirrhosis. Initial/next to diagnose fatty liver or cirrhosis is ultrasound (B). Gold standard to diagnose fatty liver or cirrhosis is liver biopsy; however, is it always needed? No (can diagnose fatty liver & cirrhosis via labs, US & non-invasive methods in >90% of cases).
Other marked answers: Compiler explanation: B (ultrasound is the initial/next step)

stem: Heart failure with reduced EF and dilated cardiomyopathy on Valsartan, statin, metoprolol, spironolactone and furosemide. What to add?
why_right: This patient with HFrEF from dilated cardiomyopathy is already on an ARB (valsartan), a beta blocker (metoprolol), an MRA (spironolactone) and a diuretic. If symptoms persist in sinus rhythm with a resting heart rate ≥70 bpm despite the beta blocker, ivabradine (If channel blocker) is added to lower heart rate and reduce HF hospitalisation. It is the only option that adds benefit without harm.
why_wrong_block:
B. Bisoprolol is another beta blocker; he is already beta-blocked with metoprolol, so it would duplicate the class. It is right only for a patient not yet on a beta blocker (step 2).
C. Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine CCB with negative inotropy that worsens HFrEF; it is contraindicated.
D. Diltiazem is also a negatively inotropic non-dihydropyridine CCB, contraindicated in reduced EF.
key_concept:
HFrEF chronic therapy ladder.
  • Step 1: ACE inhibitor or ARB
  • Step 2: beta blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate)
  • Step 3: MRA (spironolactone)
  • Then ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) and SGLT2 inhibitor
  • Ivabradine: sinus rhythm, EF ≤35%, HR ≥70 despite max beta blocker
  • Avoid: verapamil, diltiazem
exam_pearl: If ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or an SGLT2 inhibitor is offered, current guidelines put those before ivabradine; among these options, ivabradine is the only add-on.

stem: A patient with Burkitt lymphoma (DLBCL in another recall) is receiving B-CHOP chemotherapy. Laboratory results show hyperkalemia (5.3) and hypocalcemia + hyperphosphatemia. No mention of "unable to urinate". Uric acid below 480 (100% sure). No mention of hydration. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Chemotherapy for a high-grade lymphoma (Burkitt/DLBCL) with hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia is tumor lysis syndrome. Here the uric acid is not raised ("below 480") and there is no oliguria, so the abnormality left to target among these options is the high phosphate, which is what drags the calcium down. Sevelamer is a phosphate binder that lowers phosphate and so also protects against calcium-phosphate precipitation in the kidney.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lasix (furosemide): in TLS a loop diuretic is added only after adequate IV hydration to maintain urine output or treat fluid overload; it does not correct phosphate, and there is no oliguria or overload described.
B. Thiazide: lowers urinary calcium and is used for hypercalciuria and stone prevention; it has no role in TLS and can worsen the picture by causing volume depletion.
C. Allopurinol: prevents new uric acid formation and is the choice for TLS prophylaxis or hyperuricemia; here the uric acid is explicitly not high, so it does not address the presenting abnormality.
key_concept:
TLS = high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, LOW calcium; treat each abnormality.
  • Cornerstone: aggressive IV hydration
  • High uric acid: allopurinol (prevention) or rasburicase (established)
  • High phosphate: phosphate binder (e.g. sevelamer)
  • High K: standard hyperkalemia protocol
  • Low calcium: treat only if symptomatic (giving calcium with high phosphate risks precipitation)
  • Refractory or AKI: dialysis
exam_pearl: If the uric acid were high, allopurinol or rasburicase would be the answer; the stem's "uric acid below 480" is what steers you to the phosphate binder.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presented to the clinic with polyarthralgia affecting distal and proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally for 3 years. She does not have significant early morning stiffness. Clinical examination revealed no active arthritis but there were non-tender hard nodules over some distal interphalangeal joints (see lab results). Hb 140; platelets 190; WBC 11; ESR 15; CRP 5 (<8.2 mg/L); Rheumatoid factor 30 (<58 kIU/L); urea 4; creatinine 75. Which of the following is the most likely rheumatological disease?
highlight_terms_source: does not have significant early morning stiffness
non-tender hard nodules over some distal interphalangeal
why_right: Bilateral DIP and PIP pain for 3 years with no significant morning stiffness, no active arthritis and hard, non-tender DIP nodules (Heberden nodes) is the classic picture of nodal hand osteoarthritis. The labs are reassuring: normal CRP, ESR and RF, so there is no inflammatory process to explain the symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis: RA spares the DIP joints, targets MCP/PIP/wrist with soft synovial swelling and morning stiffness longer than 30 minutes, usually with raised ESR/CRP; none of these are present.
C. Polyarticular gout: presents as recurrent acute attacks of hot, red, very painful joints with raised inflammatory markers and high uric acid; tophi appear after years of attacks. This is a painless 3-year bony nodule pattern with no attacks and normal labs.
D. Reactive arthritis: an acute, asymmetric, mostly lower-limb oligoarthritis after a GI or urinary infection, often with enthesitis or conjunctivitis; not a 3-year symmetric DIP pattern.
key_concept:
Hand OA vs RA:
  • OA: DIP + PIP + thumb base; Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) bony nodes
  • OA: stiffness under 30 min, pain worse with use
  • RA: MCP + PIP + wrist, DIP spared, soft boggy swelling
  • RA: stiffness over 30 min, raised ESR/CRP, RF/anti-CCP often positive
  • OA is a clinical diagnosis with normal labs
exam_pearl: DIP involvement plus hard bony nodules points to OA; RA almost never involves the DIP joints.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B, MG. Two hand photos follow (nodal hand OA-like deformities); a Telegram caption with the second photo says (Arabic) the image came in the exam and the scenario clearly pointed to seronegative arthritis.

stem: 52 year old DM patient complaint of DIP and PIP pain and swelling with bilateral knee pain. Physical examination: DIP, PIP swelling and left knee flexion limitation. Rheumatoid factor 55 (normal <58), ESR 15 (normal <10). What is the diagnosis? (the pic of hand was mentioned)
highlight_terms_source: DIP and PIP pain and swelling
why_right: A 52-year-old with DIP and PIP swelling plus knee pain and limited knee flexion has the typical distribution of osteoarthritis (hand nodes plus a weight-bearing joint). The RF is normal (55, below the cut-off) and the ESR is only marginally raised (15), which does not support an inflammatory arthritis. DIP involvement in particular argues for OA over RA.
why_wrong_block: A. Seronegative RA: RA characteristically spares the DIP joints and gives symmetric MCP/wrist synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness and clearly raised inflammatory markers; a normal RF alone does not make an OA picture into RA.
key_concept:
Joint distribution decides OA vs RA.
  • OA: DIP, PIP, thumb base, knees, hips, spine
  • RA: MCP, PIP, wrists, MTPs; DIP spared
  • Seronegative RA still has inflammatory features (stiffness over 30 min, high ESR/CRP)
  • OA labs are normal or near normal
exam_pearl: Do not let a "borderline" lab value pull you toward seronegative RA when the DIP joints are involved.

stem: 29-year-old man is seen in the pre-employment clinic for routine exam. He is asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed a pansystolic murmur that radiated to the axilla. Which of the following is the most likely cause for this murmur?
highlight_terms_source: pansystolic murmur that radiated to the axilla
key_concept:
Cause of MR by context:
  • Young, endemic region or rheumatic history: rheumatic MR
  • Mid-systolic click + late systolic murmur: MVP
  • Older with MI or coronary disease: ischemic MR (papillary muscle)
  • Dilated LV / heart failure: functional MR
  • Fever + new murmur: infective endocarditis
exam_pearl: Decide by the extra clue: click with late systolic murmur means MVP; rheumatic history or endemic region means rheumatic; prior MI means ischemic; dilated LV means functional.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 19-year-old has history of seizure, had another brief seizure episode in the ambulance; while being examined the patient has another generalized tonic-clonic seizure which terminates after intravenous lorazepam. Which of the following is the next step in the management?
why_right: Repeated generalized seizures in quick succession (one in the ambulance, then another "while being examined") is a seizure cluster that behaves as status epilepticus. Lorazepam aborts the current seizure but its effect is short, so the next step is a second-line long-acting antiseizure drug to prevent recurrence; fosphenytoin infusion is the classic choice. Stabilisation and seizure control come before diagnostic tests.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI brain: useful later to look for a structural cause, but it is not done before seizure control; in an acute or trauma setting, CT is the imaging of choice (a variant of this recall with trauma keys CT brain).
B. Continuous EEG: indicated when the patient does not regain consciousness after the seizure stops (suspected non-convulsive status) or is paralysed or sedated; it is not the next step before giving a second-line drug.
C. Lumbar puncture: right when fever, meningism or suspected CNS infection is present, and only after imaging excludes raised intracranial pressure; nothing here suggests infection.
key_concept:
Status epilepticus ladder:
  • 0 to 5 min: ABC, oxygen, check glucose
  • 5 to 10 min: benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam or IM midazolam), may repeat once
  • Then: second-line agent (fosphenytoin/phenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam)
  • Refractory: anaesthetic agents with intubation and ICU
  • Investigate cause (glucose, electrolytes, CT if trauma or focal signs) alongside
exam_pearl: If the stem adds head trauma and CT is offered, the recall source favoured CT brain; without trauma, prevent recurrence with fosphenytoin.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Another recall (seizure in ambulance): options differed, included CT brain, not clear if phenytoin present; symptoms started after trauma. Alhomrani: benzodiazepines rapidly abort the seizure, phenytoin prevents recurrence within hours (you need both). Since he is after trauma, CT is a must. What if both phenytoin & CT present?
Other marked answers: Alhomrani (trauma version): CT brain

stem: Short scenario with no complaints, no much details except that pt had blood transfusions 10 years ago. Labs: AST and ALT within normal range. Hepatitis B serology (I am sure of every word): HBsAg (+), IgM HBc (-), IgG HBc (+), HBeAg (+), HBe antibodies (-). What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: AST and ALT within normal range
why_right: HBsAg positive means current infection, and anti-HBc IgG positive with IgM negative means the infection is not acute; with a transfusion 10 years ago this is chronic hepatitis B. Normal AST/ALT with no symptoms is why the key labels it "inactive". ("HPV" in the options is a typo for HBV.)
why_wrong_block:
A. Acute infection: needs anti-HBc IgM positive, usually with markedly raised transaminases; IgM is negative and enzymes are normal here.
C. Immunized HBV: vaccination gives anti-HBs only, with HBsAg and anti-HBc negative; this patient is HBsAg positive.
D. Recovered HBV: requires HBsAg negative with anti-HBs and anti-HBc IgG positive; persistent HBsAg rules out recovery.
key_concept:
HBV serology:
  • HBsAg+ = current infection (acute or chronic)
  • Anti-HBc IgM+ = acute; IgG+ with HBsAg+ = chronic
  • Anti-HBs + anti-HBc IgG, HBsAg negative = recovered (natural immunity)
  • Anti-HBs only = vaccinated
  • HBeAg+ = active replication, high infectivity; anti-HBe+ = low replication
exam_pearl: IgM anti-HBc is the single marker that separates acute from chronic infection when HBsAg is positive.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed options say 'HPV' (typo for HBV). Screenshot version: positive HBsAg, negative HBsAb, positive HBcAb IgG, negative HBcAb IgM, positive HBeAg, negative HBeAb; options A. Immune B. Chronic inactive hepatitis C. Recovered D. Acute active hepatitis (unmarked).

stem: 18 years old female diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and atrial fibrillation, complaining of palpitations and mild dyspnea (some vitals and elevated heart rate); asking about how to control her rhythm.
why_right: In WPW with atrial fibrillation, the danger is that blocking the AV node pushes impulses down the accessory pathway, which can cause ventricular fibrillation. The question asks how to control her rhythm, and this recall's key is amiodarone because it is the only option that is a rhythm-control drug and not a pure AV-nodal blocker. The other three options all slow the AV node and are contraindicated in pre-excited AF.
why_wrong_block:
A. Beta-blocker: a rate-control AV-nodal blocker; in pre-excited AF it can favour conduction down the accessory pathway. Right for rate control of ordinary AF without WPW.
C. Digoxin: blocks the AV node and may shorten the accessory pathway refractory period, so it is contraindicated in WPW. Right for rate control of AF with heart failure.
D. Verapamil: a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (AV-nodal blocker), contraindicated in WPW with AF because it can precipitate VF. Right for rate control of ordinary AF or for narrow-complex SVT.
key_concept:
WPW + AF: avoid AV-nodal blockers ("ABCD": adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin).
  • Unstable: synchronized DC cardioversion
  • Stable: drug acting on the accessory pathway (procainamide or ibutilide in guidelines)
  • Definitive: catheter ablation of the accessory pathway
  • Ordinary AF rhythm control: amiodarone
exam_pearl: In any AF question, a mention of WPW (short PR, delta wave) removes every AV-nodal blocker from the options.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related Q: 40-year-old with palpitations 4 h, AF with controlled rate, converted to sinus rhythm; drug to maintain sinus rhythm: A. Digoxin B. Bisoprolol C. Verapamil D. Amiodarone. Answer: D. Amiodarone.

stem: Image like this and it contains sickle cells. Ask about confirmatory test.
why_right: Sickle cells on the smear suggest sickle cell disease, but the smear alone does not prove the genotype. The confirmatory test for a hemoglobinopathy is Hb electrophoresis (or HPLC), which shows a high HbS with absent or markedly reduced HbA, and separates disease from trait and compound states.
why_wrong_block:
B. Osmotic fragility test: the initial test for hereditary spherocytosis (spherocytes on the smear), confirmed by EMA binding; it does not identify abnormal hemoglobin.
C. Bone marrow: right for suspected leukemia or marrow failure (pancytopenia, blasts); it is invasive and not used to diagnose sickle cell disease.
key_concept:
Smear finding to confirmatory test:
  • Sickle cells: Hb electrophoresis
  • Spherocytes: osmotic fragility, then EMA binding
  • Target cells / microcytosis with normal iron: Hb electrophoresis (thalassemia)
  • Blasts or pancytopenia: bone marrow
exam_pearl: SCD electrophoresis: HbS very high with HbA very low or absent; trait shows roughly half HbA and less HbS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Image shown: peripheral smear labelled 'Sickle cell in SCA'.

stem: A 66-year-old man known case of DM presented with cough and SOB, disoriented to time and place, BP: 80/55, RR: 33 and urea is 12 mmol/L, what is the calculated CURB-65 score?
why_right: Score each item: Confusion (disoriented) = 1; Urea 12 mmol/L (above 7) = 1; RR 33 (30 or more) = 1; BP 80/55 (systolic below 90, diastolic 60 or less) = 1; Age 66 (65 or more) = 1. Total = 5, the maximum score, meaning severe pneumonia needing hospital admission with ICU assessment.
why_wrong_block:
A. 2: would mean only two criteria are met; here all five are present.
B. 3: would require two criteria to be absent; here confusion, urea above 7, RR 30 or more, low BP and age 65 or more are all present.
C. 4: misses one criterion, most often the age (66 counts) or the BP (80/55 qualifies; low systolic or diastolic scores a single point).
key_concept:
CURB-65 (1 point each):
  • C: new confusion
  • U: urea above 7 mmol/L
  • R: RR 30 or more
  • B: SBP below 90 or DBP 60 or less
  • 65: age 65 or more
  • 0 to 1 outpatient; 2 ward admission; 3 or more severe, consider ICU
exam_pearl: Diabetes is not part of CURB-65; it is a distractor in the stem.
compiler_note: Compiler note: CURB-65: Confusion; Urea > 7 mmol/L; RR >= 30; BP systolic < 90 or diastolic <= 60; Age >= 65. 0-1 outpatient, 2 general ward, >=3 consider ICU.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years. She takes insulin and does smoke. She was recently started on enalapril 10 mg daily for hypertension but could not tolerate it because of a cough (see lab results). Blood pressure 160/95 mmHg Heart rate 84 /min Test Result Normal Value Creatinine 142 44-115 umol/L 24 Urine Analysis: Test Result Normal Values Creatinine clearance 66 100-140 mL/min 24-hour urine protein 1500 0-150 mg/24 hr Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
highlight_terms_source: could not tolerate it because of a cough
key_concept:
Diabetes plus proteinuria means RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor or ARB) for renoprotection.
  • ACE inhibitor cough (bradykinin) → switch to ARB
  • Angioedema on ACE inhibitor → be cautious with ARB too
  • Never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB
  • CCB or thiazide are add-ons if BP stays high
  • Monitor creatinine and potassium after starting
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Angiotensin receptor blocker.
exam_pearl: Cough on enalapril is a class effect of ACE inhibitors: swap to an ARB, do not switch to another ACE inhibitor.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 30-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with an acute monoarthritis where joint aspiration was performed. Based on the presence of crystals in the synovial fluid, he was diagnosed with gout. Which of the following is the most likely type of the crystals seen?
why_right: The stem already gives the diagnosis: gout diagnosed from synovial crystals. Gout crystals are monosodium urate, which are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent under polarized light. This is the pairing to memorize; the other options mix in features of calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout).
why_wrong_block:
B. Needle-shaped, weakly positively birefringent: the shape fits urate but the birefringence does not; weak positive birefringence belongs to CPPD.
C. Rhomboidal-shaped, negatively birefringent: rhomboid shape is CPPD, and CPPD is positively, not negatively, birefringent; this mixes the two.
D. Rhomboidal-shaped, weakly positively birefringent: these are calcium pyrophosphate crystals, the answer when the diagnosis is pseudogout.
key_concept:
Crystal pairs: gout = needle + negative; pseudogout = rhomboid + weakly positive.
  • Gout: monosodium urate, first MTP, punched-out erosions
  • Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate, knee, chondrocalcinosis
  • Acute gout: NSAID first (colchicine or steroids if contraindicated)
  • Classic exam rule: do not start allopurinol during an acute attack; if already on it, continue it
exam_pearl: Mnemonic: Gout is Negative and Needle (both N); Pseudogout is Positive and rhomboid.

stem: What test result is significant or diagnostic for uti?
why_right: A urine culture is significant when it grows a single organism at ≥10^5 CFU/mL from a clean catch midstream sample. One uropathogen in high count reflects true bladder infection rather than skin or perineal contamination.
why_wrong_block: A. Mixed bacteria in urine culture: growth of several organisms usually means the sample was contaminated during collection; the right step is to repeat a properly collected sample, not to diagnose UTI.
key_concept:
Significant bacteriuria = one organism at high colony count.
  • Clean catch midstream: ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single organism
  • Suprapubic aspirate: any growth is significant
  • Catheter sample: lower thresholds are accepted
  • Mixed growth → contamination, repeat sample
  • Positive culture without symptoms = asymptomatic bacteriuria; treat only in pregnancy or before urologic procedures
exam_pearl: A positive culture is not always a UTI to treat: without symptoms in a non-pregnant patient it is asymptomatic bacteriuria.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0882).

stem: A 50-year-old man referred to the clinic with positive HCV. He is asymptomatic with no history of drug use or previous blood transfusion. Physical examination was unremarkable. Reviewing of his lab test showed normal LFT with positive anti-HCV (ELISA), Hepatitis C RNA was negative. US abdomen showed normal liver. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Positive anti-HCV with negative HCV RNA means either resolved past infection or a false positive antibody, not active hepatitis C. He is asymptomatic with no risk exposure, normal LFTs and a normal liver on ultrasound, so he needs reassurance and no further testing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver fibroscan: used to stage fibrosis in confirmed chronic HCV (positive RNA) before treatment; there is no active infection here to stage.
C. Triphasic CT scan of liver: used to characterize a liver mass or suspected HCC, typically in cirrhosis; his liver is normal on ultrasound.
D. Repeat HCV RNA in 6 months: appropriate if there was a recent exposure (window period) or ongoing risk; this man has no exposure history and normal enzymes.
key_concept:
HCV antibody tells you exposure; HCV RNA tells you current infection.
  • Ab+ / RNA+ → active infection: assess fibrosis, genotype, treat with DAAs
  • Ab+ / RNA− → cleared infection or false positive
  • Ab+ / RNA− with no exposure and normal enzymes → reassure, no further tests
  • Ab+ / RNA− with recent exposure → repeat RNA later
exam_pearl: A recent exposure (needle stick, new IV drug use) turns Ab+/RNA− from reassurance into repeat RNA testing.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1487).

stem: A 70-year-old woman was admitted 1 week ago to the Intensive Care Unit with pneumonia requiring intubation, intravenous fluids, and dopamine support for her blood pressure. On physical examination, her skin is warm and dry, no proptosis, examination of the neck shows a normal-sized thyroid without nodules. Labs: TSH 0.1 (low), T3 2 (low), T4 11 or 14 (normal). What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A critically ill patient (ICU, pneumonia, intubated, on dopamine) with low T3, normal T4 and a low TSH, a normal thyroid and no eye signs, has euthyroid sick syndrome. Low T3 is its earliest and most common finding, and dopamine (like steroids) suppresses TSH, explaining the low TSH without true hyperthyroidism.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves disease: low TSH with HIGH T4/T3, diffuse goiter and eye signs such as proptosis; here T3 is low, the gland is normal and there is no proptosis.
B. Subacute thyroiditis: painful tender thyroid after a viral illness with high T4, low TSH and raised ESR; here the neck is normal and T3 is low.
D. Hashimoto thyroiditis: primary hypothyroidism with HIGH TSH and low T4, often with a goiter; here TSH is low, not high.
key_concept:
Euthyroid sick syndrome = abnormal thyroid tests from non-thyroidal illness, not thyroid disease.
  • Earliest and commonest: low T3 (reduced T4 to T3 conversion, high reverse T3)
  • Severe or prolonged illness: low T4 as well
  • TSH normal or low; dopamine and glucocorticoids suppress TSH
  • No treatment; recheck tests after recovery
exam_pearl: Do not diagnose hyperthyroidism from a low TSH in an ICU patient on dopamine when T3 is low and T4 is not raised.

stem: Female pt was prescribed prednisolone 60 mg tapering for 6 weeks but she continued the same dose by mistake without taper, Found dead in bathroom What is the Cause?
why_right: This recall's key is hypertensive cerebral hemorrhage. She did not stop the steroid, so this is not adrenal crisis; she stayed on a high dose (60 mg) for 6 weeks, and prolonged high-dose glucocorticoid causes sodium and fluid retention and hypertension, which the key links to a sudden fatal intracerebral bleed (found dead suddenly).
why_wrong_block:
A. Perforated duodenal ulcer: steroids can mask peritonitis, so this is the main rival, but perforation typically gives a period of severe abdominal pain rather than sudden unexplained death; it is the answer when the stem describes abdominal pain or free air in a patient on steroids, often with NSAIDs.
C. Acute cerebral vasculitis: steroids are a treatment for vasculitis, not a cause of it.
D. Intestinal ischemia with perforation: suggested by an elderly patient with AF or vascular disease and pain out of proportion to examination; it is not a recognized consequence of continuing prednisolone.
key_concept:
Know which steroid error causes which complication.
  • Abrupt stop after long use → adrenal crisis (hypotension, shock)
  • Continued high dose → hypertension, hyperglycemia, fluid retention
  • Steroids (especially with NSAIDs) → peptic ulcer, with masked peritoneal signs
  • Long term → osteoporosis, myopathy, infection, Cushingoid features
exam_pearl: If the stem says she STOPPED the steroid suddenly, think adrenal crisis; if she continued the high dose, think of the excess steroid effects.

stem: A 33-year-old man presented with 2-weeks of lethargy, fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and cough. History revealed he is a business man travels frequently to Far East. On examination, he has oral candidiasis (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: RBC 4 (4.7-6.1 x 10^12/L Male, 4.2-5.4 Female); Hb 13 (130-170 g/L Male, 120-160 g/L Female); Platelets count 145 (150-400 x 10^9/L); WBC 11 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L); Neutrophils 22 (40-60%); Lymphocytes 69 (20-40%); Monocytes 9 (2-8%). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A young man with frequent travel to the Far East (risk exposure), fever, lethargy and generalized lymphadenopathy for 2 weeks and oral candidiasis has HIV until proven otherwise. Oral thrush in an otherwise healthy adult signals impaired cell-mediated immunity, and the nonspecific febrile illness with lymphadenopathy fits HIV infection.
why_wrong_block:
B. Syphilis: secondary syphilis gives fever, lymphadenopathy and a palms and soles rash after a painless genital chancre; it does not cause oral candidiasis.
C. Brucellosis: suggested by raw milk or animal contact with undulant fever, sweats, back or sacroiliac pain and hepatosplenomegaly; no such exposure or immune deficiency sign here.
D. Toxoplasmosis: in immunocompetent adults it causes a mild mononucleosis-like illness with lymphadenopathy, and in AIDS it causes ring-enhancing brain lesions; it does not explain oral thrush.
key_concept:
Oral candidiasis in a healthy adult = check for HIV.
  • HIV clues: risk exposure, fever, generalized painless lymphadenopathy, weight loss
  • Opportunistic hints: oral thrush, recurrent zoster, TB
  • Next step: HIV antigen/antibody (4th generation) test
  • Acute HIV can mimic mononucleosis
exam_pearl: Thrush in an adult who is not diabetic, on steroids, inhaled steroids or antibiotics points to immunosuppression, classically HIV.

stem: Rt upper limb weakness post neck extension, mri brain normal What investigation will help to reach diagnosis
key_concept:
Normal brain imaging with limb weakness: look below the skull.
  • Neck extension in an older patient with spondylosis → central cord syndrome, arms weaker than legs → MRI cervical spine
  • Radicular arm pain and weakness → MRI cervical spine
  • Transient weakness with vascular risk factors (TIA) → carotid duplex first
  • Trauma with suspected fracture → CT cervical spine
exam_pearl: Decide by the pattern: transient weakness with vascular risk factors → carotid duplex; persistent arm weakness after neck extension in a spondylotic neck → MRI cervical spine; trauma with possible fracture → CT cervical spine.

stem: A 55-year-old man is evaluated 2 days after having an episode of left arm weakness without pain that lasted 5 minutes. He is now asymptomatic. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia. Medications are aspirin, insulin, and atorvastatin. Physical examination shows that no carotid bruits or cardiac murmurs are heard on cardiac auscultation, and all other physical examination findings are normal (see report). Electrocardiogram: Normal sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial imaging test?
highlight_terms_source: left arm weakness without pain that lasted 5 minutes
why_right: A 5 minute episode of left arm weakness that fully resolved is a TIA in the anterior (carotid) circulation. With diabetes and dyslipidemia, large artery atherosclerosis is the likely source, and the stem stresses sinus rhythm and no murmur, making a cardioembolic source less likely. Carotid duplex is the noninvasive, quick initial imaging test, and finding a significant symptomatic stenosis changes management (endarterectomy).
why_wrong_block:
A. Transesophageal echocardiography: right when a cardioembolic source is suspected (AF, murmur, prosthetic valve, young patient with no vascular risk factors) or a first echo is unrevealing; not the initial test here.
C. CT angiography of the neck: accurate, but needs iodinated contrast and radiation; it is used to confirm or characterize a stenosis found on duplex, or when duplex is unavailable or inconclusive, so it is not the initial test.
D. MRI of the brain: diffusion MRI is part of a full TIA workup, but the question asks for the initial imaging test to find the treatable large artery cause, which is carotid duplex.
key_concept:
TIA workup: find the source that changes management.
  • Carotid territory symptoms (arm/face weakness, aphasia, amaurosis) + atherosclerotic risk: carotid duplex first
  • Symptomatic stenosis 70 to 99 percent: carotid endarterectomy (50 to 69 percent: selected patients)
  • ECG/Holter: look for AF
  • Echo (TTE then TEE): suspected cardioembolism
  • Start antiplatelet and statin
exam_pearl: Murmur or AF in the stem pushes you to echo; vascular risk factors with sinus rhythm push you to carotid duplex.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of fatigue and lethargy. Examination reveals pallor but no organomegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to order next?
OptD: No Further Screening Should Be Done
why_right: A 55-year-old man with fatigue and pallor: in the original question the labs show microcytic iron deficiency anemia (low MCV, low ferritin, high TIBC). Iron deficiency in a man or postmenopausal woman means occult GI blood loss, and colorectal cancer must be excluded; colonoscopy (with upper endoscopy) is ideal, but among these options the test that looks for the bleeding source is the fecal occult blood test.
why_wrong_block:
A. A blood smear describes the anemia (microcytic, hypochromic) but does not find its cause; iron studies have already established iron deficiency.
C. Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when iron deficiency is confirmed by ferritin; it is for unexplained cytopenias or suspected marrow disease.
D. Unexplained iron deficiency anemia at 55 is a red flag for colorectal cancer and must always be investigated.
key_concept:
Iron deficiency anemia in an adult man (or postmenopausal woman) = GI blood loss until proven otherwise.
  • Labs: low MCV, low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC
  • Best workup: colonoscopy + upper endoscopy
  • If endoscopy not offered: fecal occult blood test
  • Marrow biopsy only for unexplained cytopenias
exam_pearl: If colonoscopy is among the options, pick it over FOBT; FOBT wins only when endoscopy is not offered.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of fatigue and lethargy. Examination reveals pallor but no organomegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to order next?
why_right: This recall is abbreviated: the full question gives labs of iron deficiency anemia (low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin). In a 55-year-old man with 3 months of fatigue and pallor, iron deficiency is presumed to be from chronic GI blood loss until proven otherwise, so the gut must be visualized directly with upper endoscopy and colonoscopy to find the source, above all colorectal or gastric cancer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Peripheral blood smear: helps characterize the anemia (microcytic, hemolysis, malignant cells) but does not find the cause of blood loss in a middle-aged man.
B. Fecal occult blood (FOB): a screening test for asymptomatic people; a negative result does not exclude a GI cause of anemia, so it is chosen only when endoscopy is not among the options.
C. Bone marrow biopsy: for unexplained cytopenias or suspected marrow disease (leukemia, myelodysplasia, infiltration); not the next test for a likely iron deficiency without organomegaly.
key_concept:
Iron deficiency anemia in a man or postmenopausal woman = GI tract until proven otherwise.
  • Investigate with bidirectional endoscopy (EGD + colonoscopy)
  • Also check celiac serology
  • FOBT is for screening, not for investigating anemia
  • If endoscopy is not offered, FOBT may be the best available option
exam_pearl: If the options include endoscopy and colonoscopy, pick it over FOBT; FOBT wins only when scopes are missing.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant of 1594 with endoscopy and colonoscopy as option D.

stem: An 85-year-old man admitted to the Intensive Care Unit following a massive stroke suddenly developed new weakness. Physical examination confirmed papilledema (see report). Emergency CT brain: Hemorrhagic transformation. Which of the following is the most definitive treatment?
why_right: A massive ischemic stroke has undergone hemorrhagic transformation, and the new weakness with papilledema means mass effect with raised intracranial pressure. The lead in asks for the "most definitive" treatment: only surgery (craniotomy and decompression) removes the mass effect, whereas medical measures merely buy time.
why_wrong_block:
A. Intravenous dexamethasone: steroids reduce vasogenic edema around tumors or abscesses; they do not help edema from stroke or intracerebral hemorrhage.
B. Administration of mannitol: an osmotic agent that temporarily lowers ICP as a bridge; it does not remove the hematoma, so it is not definitive.
D. Administering high-frequency ventilation: hyperventilation only transiently lowers ICP by vasoconstriction and is a temporizing measure, not definitive treatment.
key_concept:
Raised ICP: temporize medically, treat definitively by removing the cause.
  • Head elevation, sedation, osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline): temporizing
  • Brief hyperventilation: rescue bridge only
  • Steroids: tumor or abscess edema only, not stroke or ICH
  • Definitive for mass effect: surgical decompression or hematoma evacuation
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "initial" or "immediate" favours mannitol, while "most definitive" means surgery.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of lower back pain associated with morning stiffness lasting almost 1 hour, as well as joint pain affecting both knees and ankles bilaterally. She denied any history of skin rash or mucosal ulcerations. No history of fever. Clinical examination reveals limited lumbar spine movements and active arthritis at both knees bilaterally. She also has tenderness over the Achilles tendon (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Low back pain for 3 months with morning stiffness of about 1 hour is inflammatory back pain. Add limited lumbar spine movement, a lower limb large joint peripheral arthritis (knees, ankles) and Achilles tenderness (enthesitis) and the picture is axial spondyloarthritis, i.e. ankylosing spondylitis. The absence of rash, mucosal ulcers and fever removes the main mimics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reactive arthritis needs a preceding GI or GU infection and often conjunctivitis or urethritis; none is described here, and it is usually an acute oligoarthritis rather than chronic axial disease.
B. Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric small joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrists) that spares the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints and does not typically cause Achilles enthesitis.
D. Crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout) gives acute, episodic, very painful mono or oligoarthritis, not 3 months of inflammatory back pain with restricted lumbar movement.
key_concept:
Inflammatory back pain >3 months + enthesitis + limited lumbar motion = ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Inflammatory back pain: morning stiffness, better with activity, worse with rest, night pain
  • Peripheral: lower limb large joint arthritis (classically asymmetric oligoarthritis), Achilles enthesitis (heel pain)
  • Extra-articular: anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, apical lung fibrosis
  • Diagnosis: sacroiliitis on imaging (MRI most sensitive early), HLA-B27
  • Treatment: NSAIDs first, then TNF inhibitors
exam_pearl: A woman does not exclude AS: chronic inflammatory back pain plus enthesitis is the key, not the sex.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with increased shortness of breath on exertion, palpitations, and fatigue for one week. Physical examination reveals pale conjunctiva and splenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear shows spheroytosis (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: Spherocytes on smear have two causes: hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. A 38 year old with a new, one week history of symptomatic anemia (pallor, exertional dyspnea, palpitations) and splenomegaly fits acquired warm AIHA rather than a congenital disease. First line treatment of warm AIHA is corticosteroids, which suppress the IgG mediated splenic destruction of red cells.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transfusion only raises the hemoglobin and does not stop the autoimmune hemolysis; it is reserved for severe or unstable anemia, and crossmatching is difficult in AIHA.
B. Hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin and is used in sickle cell disease; it has no role in autoimmune hemolysis.
D. Hemolysis is not an iron deficient state (iron is recycled); parenteral iron is for iron deficiency with oral intolerance, malabsorption or ongoing loss.
key_concept:
Spherocytes in an adult with new anemia = warm AIHA until proven otherwise; treat with steroids.
  • Confirm with direct Coombs (DAT): positive for IgG with or without C3
  • Warm AIHA: steroids first, then other immunosuppression, splenectomy if refractory
  • Cold AIHA: keep warm, avoid cold; steroids work poorly
  • Hereditary spherocytosis: childhood onset, family history, jaundice, osmotic fragility or EMA binding test
exam_pearl: Spherocytes alone do not mean hereditary spherocytosis; sudden onset in an adult points to warm AIHA and steroids.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has been assessed in the Emergency Department with an acute exacerbation of asthma. Which of the following features is most likely to indicate a life-threatening attack?
OptA: Failure to improve after nebulized salbutamol 5 mg
OptB: Oxygen saturations of 94% on room air
OptC: Peak flow of 30% best or predicted
why_right: Life-threatening asthma is defined by any one of: PEF <33% of best or predicted, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, hypotension, exhaustion or confusion. A peak flow of 30% is below the 33% threshold, so it alone makes this attack life-threatening. The lead-in asks for a "life-threatening" feature, so pick the one that crosses that specific cut-off.
why_wrong_block:
A. Poor response to the first salbutamol nebulizer is not itself a life-threatening criterion; it prompts escalation (repeat SABA, ipratropium, steroids, magnesium).
B. SpO2 94% is above the life-threatening threshold, which requires saturation <92%.
D. RR 28/min (>25) is a feature of acute severe asthma, not of life-threatening asthma.
key_concept:
Acute asthma severity by PEF and signs:
  • Moderate: PEF 50 to 75%
  • Acute severe (any one): PEF 33 to 50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, cannot complete sentences
  • Life-threatening (any one): PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, arrhythmia, hypotension, exhaustion, confusion
  • Near-fatal: raised PaCO2 or need for ventilation
exam_pearl: RR ≥25 and HR ≥110 mean acute severe; PEF <33% or SpO2 <92% means life-threatening, even if the patient looks calm.

stem: A 58-year-old man known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease. His medications are metformin, sitagliptin, aspirin, lipitor, and lisinopril. He works as a car mechanic. For the last 4 months, he has started to notice exertional shortness of breath that interferes with his job but does not limit him from doing it, provided that at rest, he is fine without any shortness of breath. Which of the following is the New York Heart Association (NYHA) class of his shortness of breath?
highlight_terms_source: interferes with his job but does not limit him
why_right: NYHA class is graded purely on how much activity brings on symptoms. His dyspnea comes with ordinary exertion (his mechanic work) and "interferes with his job but does not limit him from doing it", while he is fine at rest. Ordinary activity causing symptoms with only slight limitation and comfort at rest is NYHA class II.
why_wrong_block:
A. Class I: ordinary physical activity causes no symptoms at all; he does get breathless during his normal work.
C. Class III: marked limitation, where less than ordinary activity causes symptoms and the patient cannot keep up normal work; he still manages his job.
D. Class IV: symptoms at rest or with any activity; he is explicitly fine at rest.
key_concept:
NYHA = symptoms vs level of activity:
  • I: no limitation, ordinary activity symptom free
  • II: slight limitation, ordinary activity causes symptoms, comfortable at rest
  • III: marked limitation, less than ordinary activity causes symptoms, comfortable at rest
  • IV: symptoms at rest, any activity worsens them
exam_pearl: "Can still do his job but it bothers him" = II; "cannot do ordinary activity" = III; "symptoms at rest" = IV.

stem: A 70-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department complaining of increasing shortness of breath and a productive cough for the past 5 months. He has been a smoker for over 50 years. Over the course of 5 months, he complained of malaise, night sweats, fever, and has lost 10 kg over the last 3 months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 70 year old with over 50 years of smoking, 5 months of progressive dyspnea and productive cough, plus constitutional symptoms (malaise, night sweats, fever) and 10 kg weight loss over 3 months fits lung carcinoma. The chronic time course and marked weight loss in an elderly heavy smoker outweigh an infective or reactive airway cause.
why_wrong_block:
B. Pneumonia is an acute illness of days with fever and productive cough; it does not explain 5 months of progression with 10 kg weight loss (a nonresolving pneumonia in a smoker should itself raise suspicion of an obstructing tumor).
C. Asthma gives episodic wheeze, dry cough and dyspnea, often from youth, without fever, night sweats or weight loss.
D. Pulmonary embolism presents with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain and tachycardia, not a 5 month course with productive cough and B symptoms.
key_concept:
Elderly heavy smoker + months of cough/dyspnea + weight loss = lung cancer until proven otherwise.
  • Acute fever + productive cough over days: pneumonia
  • Chronic productive cough in a smoker without weight loss: COPD/chronic bronchitis
  • Night sweats + fever + hemoptysis with TB exposure: consider tuberculosis
  • Sudden dyspnea + pleuritic pain + risk factors: PE
exam_pearl: Fever and night sweats tempt you toward TB or pneumonia, but age, heavy smoking and major weight loss make carcinoma the best answer when TB is not offered.

stem: case about old man no medical history only hemorrhagic stroke treated and then after 1 week there is facial asymmetry and dysthymia imaging show left cerebral infarction ask about the mechanism?
why_right: A hemorrhagic stroke followed about 1 week later by new deficits (facial asymmetry, speech disturbance) and a new cerebral infarction is delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm, the classic complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage. Vasospasm peaks roughly days 4 to 14 after the bleed and narrows the cerebral arteries enough to cause infarction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atherosclerosis: causes thrombotic stroke in patients with vascular risk factors; this man has no medical history, and the timing right after a bleed points to vasospasm.
B. Cerebral embolism: suggested by AF, valvular disease or a carotid source, with abrupt onset deficits; nothing here suggests an embolic source.
C. Rupture aneurism: explains the original hemorrhage, but rebleeding presents as a new hemorrhage with sudden headache and reduced consciousness, not an infarct.
key_concept:
Complications of subarachnoid hemorrhage by timing.
  • First days: rebleeding (prevent by securing the aneurysm)
  • Days 4 to 14: vasospasm with delayed ischemic infarction (nimodipine to prevent)
  • Any time: hydrocephalus
  • Hyponatremia (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting)
exam_pearl: New deficit with infarction after a bleed = vasospasm; new deficit with fresh blood = rebleeding.

stem: Pt understand what is being told to him, But can't write, can't remember words to respond and can't know left and right Where is lesion? (I tried to remember it as much as I can,)
why_right: Comprehension is intact ("understands what is being told"), so this is not a receptive (Wernicke) aphasia. Inability to write (agraphia) and left right confusion are core features of Gerstmann syndrome (with finger agnosia and acalculia), and word finding difficulty (anomia) also fits a lesion at the angular gyrus. All of these localise to the dominant (usually left) parietal lobe, which handles sensory integration and spatial awareness.
why_wrong_block:
B. Temporal lobe: a dominant temporal (Wernicke) lesion causes fluent speech with POOR comprehension; here comprehension is preserved. It also causes memory and auditory processing problems, not left right confusion.
C. Frontal: a dominant frontal (Broca) lesion gives non fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension, often with contralateral weakness; it does not explain left right disorientation.
D. Occipital: lesions cause visual field defects (contralateral homonymous hemianopia) or cortical blindness, not writing or spatial orientation problems.
key_concept:
Agraphia + left right confusion (± finger agnosia, acalculia) = Gerstmann syndrome = dominant parietal lobe (angular gyrus).
  • Parietal: sensation, spatial awareness, Gerstmann (dominant), neglect (non dominant)
  • Temporal: memory, hearing; Wernicke aphasia (poor comprehension)
  • Frontal: Broca aphasia, personality change, motor weakness
  • Occipital: visual field defects
  • Cerebellum: dysmetria, intention tremor
exam_pearl: If the patient could NOT understand speech, the answer would flip to the temporal lobe (Wernicke area).

stem: 28-year-old man presented to the clinic with a 2-month history of joint pain, morning stiffness and mouth ulcers. On examination, he has active arthritis at both wrist joints and second proximal interphalangeal joint of both hands (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 125 {130-170 g/L (Male) | 120-160 g/L (Female); Platelets count 220 {150-400 x 109/L; WBC 5 {4.5-10.5 x 109/L; ESR 55 {2-10 mm/h (Male) | 3-15 mm/h (Female); Urea 4.5 {2.75-7.4 mmol/L; Creatinine 78 {44-115 mol/L; C-reactive peptide 12 <8.2 mg/L Complement C3 0.9 {0.7-1.5 g/L; Complement C4 0.1 {0.15-0.45 g/L; about drug that reduces remission and vascular risk?
why_right: Arthritis, mouth ulcers, raised ESR with a near normal CRP and low C4 point to systemic lupus erythematosus. Hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone drug for every SLE patient without contraindication: it reduces flares and helps maintain remission, and it lowers thrombotic and cardiovascular (vascular) risk and improves survival. The lead in asks about remission and vascular risk, which is exactly the antimalarial benefit.
why_wrong_block:
B. Azathioprine: a steroid sparing immunosuppressant used for moderate disease or lupus nephritis maintenance; it does not carry the vascular protective benefit of hydroxychloroquine.
C. Cyclosporine: a calcineurin inhibitor reserved for refractory disease or some nephritis regimens; it causes hypertension and nephrotoxicity, so it does not reduce vascular risk.
D. Mycophenolate mofetil: first line induction for lupus nephritis (raised creatinine, proteinuria); here creatinine and urea are normal and there is no major organ involvement.
key_concept:
Every SLE patient gets hydroxychloroquine; escalate by organ involvement.
  • All SLE: hydroxychloroquine (fewer flares, lower thrombotic risk, better survival)
  • Arthritis not controlled: add low dose steroid ± methotrexate
  • Lupus nephritis: high dose steroid + mycophenolate
  • Maintenance or steroid sparing: azathioprine
  • Clue: high ESR with normal CRP, low complement = SLE activity
exam_pearl: If the stem showed raised creatinine and proteinuria, the answer would flip to mycophenolate with steroids.

stem: An elderly patient receiving IV heparin develops deep vein thrombosis 6 days post-operatively. Platelet count is 75 ×10°/L. What is the best next step in management?
why_right: A new thrombosis with a platelet fall to 75 on day 6 of heparin is heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), a prothrombotic immune reaction. Management is to stop all heparin and start a non heparin anticoagulant, typically a direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban or bivalirudin (older sources name lepirudin, now withdrawn).
why_wrong_block:
A. Start warfarin: warfarin must not be started during acute HIT because early protein C depletion can cause venous limb gangrene; it is introduced only after platelet recovery, overlapping with a non heparin agent.
B. Start enoxaparin: LMWH cross reacts with HIT antibodies and is contraindicated; it would be right for a DVT with a normal platelet count.
C. Transfuse platelets: HIT is thrombotic, not a bleeding disorder; platelet transfusion can fuel further thrombosis and is reserved for active serious bleeding.
key_concept:
Platelet fall 5 to 10 days after heparin ± new thrombosis = HIT: stop heparin, start a non heparin anticoagulant.
  • Stop ALL heparin, including flushes and LMWH
  • Start direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin; lepirudin in older texts) or fondaparinux
  • Warfarin only after platelets recover
  • No routine platelet transfusion
exam_pearl: Thrombocytopenia within the first 1 to 2 days of heparin is usually non immune and benign; the 5 to 10 day timing is the HIT clue.

stem: WHATS A SINGLE CONFIRMATORY TEST FOR IDA?
key_concept:
Ferritin is the best single blood test for IDA; bone marrow iron stain is the historical gold standard.
  • IDA: low ferritin, low iron, HIGH TIBC, high RDW
  • Anemia of chronic disease: high or normal ferritin, low iron, LOW TIBC
  • Thalassemia trait: normal ferritin, normal RDW, raised HbA2 in beta trait
  • Absent marrow iron stores = definitive, rarely needed
exam_pearl: If "bone marrow" is an option and the lead in says gold standard or most definitive, that beats ferritin.

stem: Q: Most definitive test to diagnose underlying disease (labs showed microcytic anemia).
why_right: The lead in asks for the most definitive test for the underlying cause of a microcytic anemia. A bone marrow aspirate with iron (Prussian blue) stain directly shows absent iron stores in iron deficiency, normal or increased stores in anemia of chronic disease, and ring sideroblasts in sideroblastic anemia, so it is the gold standard. It is invasive and rarely needed in practice, but "most definitive" points to it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Serum Iron: low in both iron deficiency and anemia of chronic disease and varies with time of day, so it cannot define the cause.
B. Serum ferritin: the best first line, non invasive test (low ferritin is near diagnostic of IDA), but it is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal with inflammation; right when the question asks for the most useful or initial test.
C. TIBC: helps separate IDA (high) from anemia of chronic disease (low) but is an indirect marker, not definitive.
key_concept:
Initial or best non invasive test = ferritin; most definitive or gold standard = bone marrow iron stain.
  • Microcytic causes: iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease, lead, sideroblastic
  • Low ferritin, high TIBC: IDA
  • High ferritin, low TIBC: anemia of chronic disease
  • Normal iron studies with microcytosis: thalassemia, check Hb electrophoresis
  • Ring sideroblasts on marrow: sideroblastic anemia
exam_pearl: The lead in verb decides it: "initial" or "most appropriate" is ferritin, "most definitive" is bone marrow.

stem: A long case straightforward about SCD; the question asks which of the following, if absent in electrophoresis, enables you to diagnose it?
why_right: In sickle cell disease (HbSS) the beta chain gene produces only HbS, so normal adult HbA is absent on electrophoresis, with HbS predominant and HbF often raised. The absence of HbA is what separates disease from sickle cell trait, in which HbA is still present alongside HbS.
why_wrong_block:
A. HB S: HbS is PRESENT and predominant in sickle cell disease; its absence would exclude the diagnosis.
C. HB F: HbF is normal or raised in SCD (and markedly raised in beta thalassemia major); it is not absent.
D. HB C: HbC is present only in HbSC disease; its absence is expected in HbSS and does not make the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Electrophoresis: no HbA + HbS predominant = sickle cell disease.
  • SCD: HbA absent, HbS high, HbF normal or raised, HbA2 normal
  • Sickle trait: HbA present (more than HbS), HbS under 50%
  • Beta thal major: HbA absent, HbF markedly raised, no HbS
  • Beta thal trait: raised HbA2
  • HbSC: HbS + HbC, no HbA
exam_pearl: Presence of BOTH HbA and HbS means sickle cell trait, not disease.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset fatigue, generalized weakness, no jaundice; she denies recent infections or new medications. On physical examination, no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly is noted. Investigations reveal the following: Hemoglobin: Low; Reticulocyte count: Elevated; Platelet count: Normal; Indirect bilirubin: Elevated; Haptoglobin: Decreased. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Low Hb, raised reticulocytes, raised indirect bilirubin and low haptoglobin confirm hemolysis, and the normal platelet count rules out a microangiopathic or consumptive process. A sudden onset in a previously well 35 year old with no splenomegaly, no new drugs and no infection fits an acquired immune cause, autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Confirm with a positive direct Coombs test.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH): intravascular hemolysis with dark morning urine, often cytopenias and unusual venous thromboses; right when hemoglobinuria, pancytopenia or thrombosis are given.
B. Hereditary Spherocytosis: a lifelong inherited hemolysis with family history, splenomegaly, jaundice and pigment gallstones, usually recognised in childhood; a sudden adult onset without splenomegaly does not fit.
D. DIC: consumes platelets and clotting factors, so platelets would be LOW with prolonged PT and APTT, in a patient with sepsis, trauma or malignancy; here platelets are normal.
key_concept:
Hemolysis markers: high retics, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH, LOW haptoglobin; then find the cause.
  • Acute adult onset, Coombs +: AIHA (warm = IgG, steroids)
  • Chronic, family history, splenomegaly, gallstones, spherocytes: hereditary spherocytosis
  • Hemoglobinuria, cytopenias, thrombosis: PNH
  • Low platelets + abnormal coagulation: DIC
  • Low platelets + normal coagulation + schistocytes: TTP or HUS
exam_pearl: Add jaundice with gallstones (chronic hemolysis) to the same stem and the keyed answer flips to hereditary spherocytosis, as in the companion card.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden fatigue, generalized weakness, and jaundice. He denies infections or new medications. On exam, he is mildly icteric with no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Lab findings include low hemoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count, normal platelet count, elevated indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin. Abdominal ultrasound shows multiple gallstones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The labs show hemolysis (raised reticulocytes and indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin) with normal platelets. The decisive extra clue is multiple gallstones with jaundice: pigment stones form only after longstanding hemolysis, which points to an inherited membrane defect, hereditary spherocytosis, rather than a new acquired process. Confirm with spherocytes on smear, a negative direct Coombs test and osmotic fragility or EMA binding.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH): presents with dark morning urine, cytopenias and venous thrombosis rather than gallstones; right when hemoglobinuria or unusual thrombosis is described.
C. Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA): acquired, often abrupt hemolysis with a positive direct Coombs test; gallstones imply years of hemolysis, which favours the inherited disorder.
D. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC): platelets would be low with prolonged clotting times in a sick patient; the normal platelet count excludes it.
key_concept:
Pigment gallstones in a young adult = chronic hemolysis; think hereditary spherocytosis.
  • HS: family history, jaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones, spherocytes, high MCHC
  • HS tests: osmotic fragility, confirmed by EMA binding; Coombs negative
  • Spherocytes differential: HS vs warm AIHA (Coombs separates them)
  • Definitive HS treatment when severe: splenectomy (± cholecystectomy)
exam_pearl: Spherocytes alone do not settle it: a positive direct Coombs test flips the diagnosis to warm AIHA.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown under number 1660 with printed 'Answer: B'. Variant of 1659 (here with jaundice and gallstones).

stem: A 50-year-old woman with major depression complains of excessive urination and thirst for 2 months. She had a right mastectomy 1 year ago. 3 months before, lung metastases was diagnosed. The physical examination is normal except for the surgical scar. BP 115/75 mmHg, HR 80/min, RR 16/min, Temp 37.1 °C. Labs: Sodium 150 (134-146 mmol/L), Potassium 3.8, Urea 6.7, Creatinine 111, Fasting blood sugar 6.8 (3.5-6.5 mmol/L). 24 h urine: Osmolality 110 (280-910 mOsm/kg H2O). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Polyuria and thirst with sodium 150 and a very dilute urine (osmolality 110) means the kidney is losing free water it should be conserving: diabetes insipidus. The breast cancer with lung metastases points to a central cause, since metastatic deposits in the posterior pituitary or stalk stop ADH release. Breast and lung cancers are the commonest metastatic causes of central DI.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adipsic hypernatremia: caused by a LOSS of thirst (hypothalamic osmoreceptor damage), so patients do not drink; this woman has excessive thirst and polyuria.
C. Psychogenic polydipsia: the depression is the bait. Water excess gives dilute urine but a LOW or low normal sodium; a sodium of 150 rules it out.
key_concept:
Polyuria with dilute urine: the serum sodium separates the causes.
  • DI: high sodium, high serum osmolality, low urine osmolality
  • Primary (psychogenic) polydipsia: dilute urine with low or normal sodium
  • Adipsic hypernatremia: high sodium WITHOUT thirst
  • SIADH (opposite): low sodium, concentrated urine, low output
  • Central DI causes include pituitary metastasis (breast, lung), head trauma, surgery
exam_pearl: Dilute urine plus HIGH sodium = DI; dilute urine plus LOW sodium = drinking too much.

stem: A 60-year-old man with hypertension presents to the ER with sudden onset retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations for 2 hours. His past medical history is significant for a non-hemorrhagic stroke 2 months ago. ECG: ST-segment elevation in II, III, aVF. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: ST-segment elevation in II, III, aVF
why_right: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with 2 hours of chest pain is an inferior STEMI that needs urgent reperfusion. Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy, and here it is the only option because his ischemic stroke 2 months ago (within 3 months) is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fibrinolysis is used when timely PCI is not available, but an ischemic stroke within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication.
B. Aspirin is given to every STEMI patient as adjunct therapy, but it is not reperfusion and does not open the occluded artery.
C. Unfractionated heparin is adjunctive anticoagulation during PCI; on its own it does not reperfuse the infarct related artery.
key_concept:
STEMI = reperfusion; primary PCI first, fibrinolysis only if PCI cannot be done in time and there is no contraindication.
  • Inferior (II, III, aVF): RCA in most
  • Absolute contraindications to lysis: prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 3 months, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, intracranial tumor
  • Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant are adjuncts
exam_pearl: A recent ischemic stroke in a STEMI stem is the clue that rules out lysis and makes PCI the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recent ischemic stroke contraindicates fibrinolysis. Related 'Q:' in the block: MI chest pain for 3 hours, not ongoing, management: A. thrombolysis B. PCI; PCI highlighted.

stem: Adult with knee pain, wrist pain, and ankle pain, I think for 5 weeks. He has a history of URTI a few weeks back before the symptoms started. Knee is swollen. Labs are fine. Synovial analysis is normal. What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: history of URTI a few weeks back
why_right: This recall's key is toxic (transient) synovitis because the joint inflammation followed a recent URTI, the labs are fine and the synovial analysis is normal, i.e. a self limiting post viral, sterile synovitis rather than infection. Between the two options, a normal joint aspirate makes the sterile, post infectious process the only fit.
why_wrong_block: A. Septic arthritis: needs an acutely hot, red joint, usually one joint, with fever, raised inflammatory markers and purulent fluid (synovial WBC typically above 50,000 with neutrophils above 75%); here labs and synovial fluid are normal.
key_concept:
Synovial fluid sorts arthritis into normal, non inflammatory, inflammatory and septic.
  • Normal: WBC below 200, clear
  • Non inflammatory (OA): WBC up to 2,000
  • Inflammatory (RA, crystals, reactive): 2,000 to 50,000
  • Septic: above 50,000, neutrophils above 75%, culture positive
  • Post infectious arthritis after URTI or GI/GU infection: sterile, often lower limb oligoarthritis
  • Transient synovitis: classically a child's hip after a viral illness, afebrile, normal labs
exam_pearl: Normal labs plus normal synovial fluid after a recent infection = sterile post infectious synovitis, never septic.
